questions.q: If man lives in “God’s country” and must live by God’s scheme, how is he to know what that scheme requires?
options: Through the opinion of the majority
Not quite. The article says: Through the prophets, whose guidance is gathered in the Quran.
Through trial and error over many generations
Not quite. The article says: Through the prophets, whose guidance is gathered in the Quran.
Through the prophets, whose guidance is gathered in the Quran
Yes. They set it out plainly for all.
Through the customs of each land
Not quite. The article says: Through the prophets, whose guidance is gathered in the Quran.
questions.rationale: “It was to provide an answer to this question that God raised up His prophets… The Quran is a collection of this prophetic guidance.”

questions.q: Resources in nature’s keeping cause no havoc; in human hands they can. What remedy does the article propose?
options: Leave all resources untouched
Not quite. The article says: Man should learn to use them as nature does – applying nature’s model with self-discipline.
Give control to a single authority
Not quite. The article says: Man should learn to use them as nature does – applying nature’s model with self-discipline.
Man should learn to use them as nature does – applying nature’s model with self-discipline
Well read. Discipline, not freedom alone, brings peace.
Develop stronger weapons for defence
Not quite. The article says: Man should learn to use them as nature does – applying nature’s model with self-discipline.
questions.rationale: “Man must learn how to utilize these resources in the way nature utilizes them. The model of nature must be applied to human life.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, has man alone been given freedom?
options: Because he could not be controlled
Not quite. The article says: So that he may choose an upright life of his own free will and so earn the highest credit.
So that he may choose an upright life of his own free will and so earn the highest credit
Right. Not to live without restraint.
So that he may enjoy himself as he likes
Not quite. The article says: So that he may choose an upright life of his own free will and so earn the highest credit.
So that he may rule over other creatures
Not quite. The article says: So that he may choose an upright life of his own free will and so earn the highest credit.
questions.rationale: “Its purpose is that man should lead a morally upright life of his own free will, thus demonstrating that he is of the highest moral character.”

questions.q: Freedom opens two doors for man. What decides which he passes through?
options: Whether he lives long or briefly
Not quite. The article says: Whether freedom makes him arrogant, or he stays humble and binds himself to God’s will.
Whether freedom makes him arrogant, or he stays humble and binds himself to God’s will
Yes. Success or failure lies in the response.
Whether he is born rich or poor
Not quite. The article says: Whether freedom makes him arrogant, or he stays humble and binds himself to God’s will.
Whether others approve of him
Not quite. The article says: Whether freedom makes him arrogant, or he stays humble and binds himself to God’s will.
questions.rationale: “If, on receiving freedom an individual becomes arrogant and insolent, it will mean that he has failed the test. If on the other hand, he remains modest and humble… he will have made the right use of his God-given freedom.”

questions.q: The article likens the seriousness the Prophet’s message demands to a particular moment. Which?
options: A traveller at night whose torch suddenly shows a snake in his path
Well read. Not a matter for idle theory.
A merchant counting his day’s takings
Not quite. The article says: A traveller at night whose torch suddenly shows a snake in his path.
A sailor sighting land
Not quite. The article says: A traveller at night whose torch suddenly shows a snake in his path.
A student opening an examination paper
Not quite. The article says: A traveller at night whose torch suddenly shows a snake in his path.
questions.rationale: “It requires every man to take a serious view of his situation—even more so than a traveller in the night whose torch reveals a black snake slithering menacingly in front of him.”

questions.q: By what single principle does the article explain human history, including the presence of suffering?
options: The principle of endless repetition
Not quite. The article says: The principle of “test” – man is placed here to be tried.
The principle of “test” – man is placed here to be tried
Correct. Neither pure determinism nor pure freedom explains it.
The principle of the survival of the strongest
Not quite. The article says: The principle of “test” – man is placed here to be tried.
The principle of chance
Not quite. The article says: The principle of “test” – man is placed here to be tried.
questions.rationale: “According to Islam, there is only one correct principle to interpret human history and that is the principle of ‘test’.”

questions.q: Why, in the article’s reasoning, did the possibility of evil have to be allowed?
options: Because good cannot exist without equal evil
Not quite. The article says: Without real freedom to do wrong, choosing good would earn no credit – and freedom can be misused.
Because evil makes life interesting
Not quite. The article says: Without real freedom to do wrong, choosing good would earn no credit – and freedom can be misused.
Without real freedom to do wrong, choosing good would earn no credit – and freedom can be misused
Well reasoned. A small price for something very precious.
Because the Creator overlooked it
Not quite. The article says: Without real freedom to do wrong, choosing good would earn no credit – and freedom can be misused.
questions.rationale: “Man can be granted the credit for a good deed only on the condition that, despite having the opportunity to indulge in bad deeds, he chooses of his own free will to act virtuously.”

questions.q: Moses was raised in Pharaoh’s palace, yet could not remain there. What does the article suggest such blocked paths may mean in our own lives?
options: That we chose wrongly and must give up
Not quite. The article says: That God has a higher purpose in view and is prompting us to rethink and re-plan.
That others are working against us
Not quite. The article says: That God has a higher purpose in view and is prompting us to rethink and re-plan.
That effort is useless
Not quite. The article says: That God has a higher purpose in view and is prompting us to rethink and re-plan.
That God has a higher purpose in view and is prompting us to rethink and re-plan
Yes. So setbacks can be received with gratitude.
questions.rationale: “If God prevents a task from happening the way you had planned it, it is a clue that He wants you to do something else.”

questions.q: In contrast to every other creature, what unique thing does the article say man must do?
options: Build cities and machines
Not quite. The article says: Live by truth he has discovered for himself, with self-imposed discipline.
Speak many languages
Not quite. The article says: Live by truth he has discovered for himself, with self-imposed discipline.
Live by truth he has discovered for himself, with self-imposed discipline
Exactly. Others obey nature’s law without choosing.
Live longer than other creatures
Not quite. The article says: Live by truth he has discovered for himself, with self-imposed discipline.
questions.rationale: “In contrast to other living beings, man must do something unique—and that is, to live in self-discovered truth.”

questions.q: The verses recall that man is created from a mere drop, yet becomes “openly contentious.” What lesson does the commentary draw?
options: That man is of no importance
Not quite. The article says: Remembering his humble origin, he would never be arrogant, and would be grateful for all he has been given.
That animals are superior to man
Not quite. The article says: Remembering his humble origin, he would never be arrogant, and would be grateful for all he has been given.
That disputes should be settled by force
Not quite. The article says: Remembering his humble origin, he would never be arrogant, and would be grateful for all he has been given.
Remembering his humble origin, he would never be arrogant, and would be grateful for all he has been given
Well read. Every benefit he enjoys was provided for him.
questions.rationale: “If he were to keep in view the reality of his origin, he would never allow himself to become arrogant in this world.”
